title: Getting Started
text:
Setup Instructions
The Pico needs to be connected to your computer through the USB cable for power (unless provided externally), to upload a program on it, and to communicate with it during the execution of the program (printing in a terminal or reading user input from keyboard).

title: Getting Started
text:
First binaries
Binaries are files that contain machine instructions for the Pico. The file extension is .uf2. When programming in C, such binary is produced on your computer and needs to be transfered to the Pico. When using micropython, the micropython interpreter is the binary that needs to be transfered to the Pico. After this, python programs can be transfered to it to be interpreted on the machine.
Here, we will follow the Your First Binaries section of the Pico tutorial to practice this step and test the Pico.
To load a program on the Pico, follow this process:

Starting from a board disconnect from the computer, press the BOOTSEL button and insert the USB connection to your computer at the same time.
The Pico should show up as a USB drive on your computer.
Copy the exectuable .uf2 file on this drive.
This should upload the program on the Pico and restart it automatically.



LED Blink
Download and install the Blink UF2 file. This file supports all Pico variants. If all goes well, you should see the integrated LED blink on your board.


USB Serial communication
Download and install the ‘Hello World’ UF2 file. This file should also supports all Pico variants. Once it is installed and running, open a Serial monitor and connect it to the port of the board. The default baud rate is 115200.


Programming environment
We recommend using Visual Studio Code for this project, both for C/C++ programming and for MicroPython.
There are extensions available that greatly facilitate the development of programs. These can normally be installed directly from the VS Code environment.

title: Interrupts
text:
Overview
There were two issues with the code we previously studied to toggle the state of an LED with a button.
The main issue was related to the debouncing - the fact that when a mechanical switch toggles, it doesn’t do it cleanly, but oscillates for a few milliseconds. Adding a wait command could help regulate this issue.
The second issue is about performance. The main loop spends lots of resources monitoring the state of a pin, just in case it changes. This is resource intensive for a task that is not very complicated for such a power chip. If only we could delegate these mundane tasks to specialised circuits. Well, we can! This is the domain of interrupts.
An interrupt is precisely a hardware feature that allows a microcontroller to react instantly to real-world events without constantly checking for them in a loop. For this, you register a special function, called an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or handler. That function is not directly called, and essentially sits dormant. When a specific hardware signal occurs, such as a voltage transition on a GPIO pin or a timer expiring, the hardware immediately pauses the main execution thread, jumps to run your interrupt handler function, and then seamlessly resumes your main program right where it left off. Interrupts respond to events, such as a change in value. They are therefore well suited for detecting the press of a button. Whether implemented in C using callbacks or in MicroPython via Pin.irq(), interrupts use dedicated hardware to monitor changes, enabling fast response and leaving your main loop free to handle other tasks, or simply sleep to conserve power.

Assignment 1: Interrupts
text:
Objective
Write a program in C or Micropython that will turn on the LED after the button is pressed 10 times.
What happens if you keep pressing afterwards is up to you.

title: Assignment 1: Interrupts
text:
Requirements

You must keep your main while loop clear, although you may use it to print information on the serial monitor if useful.
You must debounce the button at the microcontroller level, i.e. not using a low pass filter at the input. Although this might be a perfectly valid approach too outside of this exercise.
